stem: If \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR\) and \(\angle A = 60^\circ\), then \(\angle P = ?\)
solution: In \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR\), corresponding angles are congruent, so \(\angle A = \angle P\) (c.p.c.t.). \(\therefore \angle P = 60^\circ\).

stem: In right-angled \(\triangle ABC\), if \(\angle B = 90^\circ\), \(AB = 6\), \(BC = 8\), then find AC.
solution: By Pythagoras theorem, \(AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2\). \(AC = \sqrt{AB^2 + BC^2} = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10\).

stem: Write the length of the largest chord of a circle with radius 3.2 cm.
solution: The largest chord of a circle is its diameter. Length of diameter \(= 2 \times \text{radius} = 2 \times 3.2 = 6.4\) cm.

stem: From the given number line, find d(A, B).
solution: From the number line, the coordinate of A is \(-3\) and the coordinate of B is \(3\). \(d(A, B) = 3 - (-3) = 6\).
figureNote: Number line from -4 to 4 with point A marked above -3 and point B marked above 3 (page 1).

stem: Find the value of \(\sin 30^\circ + \cos 60^\circ\).

subtopic: Area of Sector and Segment of a Circle
stem: Find the area of a circle of radius 7 cm.
solution: Area of circle \(= \pi r^2 = \frac{22}{7} \times 7^2 = 154\) cm\(^2\).

stem: Draw seg AB of length 5.7 cm and bisect it.
solution: a. Draw a line segment AB measuring 5.7 cm. b. With the compass width more than half of AB and the steel end on A, draw arcs above and below AB. c. With the same width and the steel end on B, cut the previous arcs; name the intersection points X and Y. d. Join XY; it cuts AB at point M. e. M is the midpoint of AB and line XY is its perpendicular bisector.

stem: In right-angled triangle PQR, if \(\angle P = 60^\circ\), \(\angle R = 30^\circ\) and \(PR = 12\), then find the values of PQ and QR.
solution: \(\angle Q = 180^\circ - (\angle P + \angle R) = 180^\circ - 90^\circ = 90^\circ\), so \(\triangle PQR\) is a \(30^\circ\text{-}60^\circ\text{-}90^\circ\) triangle with hypotenuse \(PR = 12\) cm. QR (side opposite \(60^\circ\)) \(= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times PR = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 12 = 6\sqrt{3}\) cm. PQ (side opposite \(30^\circ\)) \(= \frac{1}{2} \times PR = \frac{1}{2} \times 12 = 6\) cm.

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: In a right circular cone, if perpendicular height is 12 cm and radius is 5 cm, then find its slant height.
solution: By Pythagoras theorem, slant height \(l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2} = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13\) cm.

subtopic: Theorem of Areas of Similar Triangles
stem: \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle DEF\) are equilateral triangles. If \(A(\triangle ABC) : A(\triangle DEF) = 1 : 2\) and \(AB = 4\), then what is the length of DE?
solution: Both triangles are equilateral, hence similar. By the theorem of areas of similar triangles, \(\frac{A(\triangle ABC)}{A(\triangle DEF)} = \frac{AB^2}{DE^2}\). \(\frac{1}{2} = \frac{4^2}{DE^2}\), so \(DE^2 = 2 \times 16 = 32\) and \(DE = \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}\). Correct option (d). [Note: the source booklet printed option (a) \(2\sqrt{2}\) via an arithmetic slip (\(DE^2 = 4 \times 2 = 8\)); the mathematically correct value is \(4\sqrt{2}\).]

stem: Out of the following, which is a Pythagorean triplet?
solution: A Pythagorean triplet satisfies (largest number)\(^2\) = sum of squares of the other two numbers. \(8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289 = 17^2\). So \((8, 15, 17)\) is a Pythagorean triplet. Correct option (c).

stem: \(\angle ACB\) is inscribed in arc ACB of a circle with centre O. If \(\angle ACB = 65^\circ\), find m(arc ACB).
solution: By the inscribed angle theorem, \(2\angle ACB = m(\text{arc ADB})\), so \(m(\text{arc ADB}) = 2 \times 65^\circ = 130^\circ\). Since the total measure of the arcs of a circle is \(360^\circ\), \(m(\text{arc ACB}) = 360^\circ - 130^\circ = 230^\circ\). Correct option (c).

stem: \(1 + \tan^2 \theta = ?\)
solution: By the trigonometric identity, \(1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta\). Correct option (b).

subtopic: Construction of a Tangent to a Circle
stem: Construct a tangent to a circle with centre A and radius 3.4 cm at any point P on it.
solution: a. With 3.4 cm in the compass, draw a circle with centre A. b. Take any point P on the circle. c. Draw ray AP and extend it. d. With a suitable compass measure, draw arcs on both sides of P along the ray. e. From these arcs, draw arcs above and below to get their point of intersection. f. Join the intersection points and extend; this line through P (perpendicular to AP) is the required tangent.

stem: Find the slope of a line passing through the points A(3, 1) and B(5, 3).

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: Find the surface area of a sphere of radius 3.5 cm.
solution: Surface area of sphere \(= 4\pi r^2 = 4 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 3.5^2 = 154\) cm\(^2\).

stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), ray BD bisects \(\angle ABC\). If A-D-C, A-E-B and seg ED \(\parallel\) side BC, then prove that \(\frac{AB}{BC} = \frac{AE}{EB}\).
solution: In \(\triangle ABC\), ray BD is the bisector of \(\angle ABC\). \(\therefore \frac{AB}{BC} = \frac{AD}{DC}\) ...(I) (by angle bisector theorem). In \(\triangle ABC\), seg DE \(\parallel\) side BC. \(\therefore \frac{AE}{EB} = \frac{AD}{DC}\) ...(II) (by Basic Proportionality Theorem). \(\therefore \frac{AB}{BC} = \frac{AE}{EB}\) (from I and II).
figureNote: \(\triangle ABC\) with ray BD bisecting \(\angle ABC\) (two angle marks at B), point E on side AB and point D on side AC, with seg ED \(\parallel\) side BC (page 2).

stem: Prove that angles inscribed in the same arc are congruent. Given: \(\angle PQR\) and \(\angle PSR\) are inscribed in the same arc, and arc PXR is intercepted by the angles. To prove: \(\angle PQR \cong \angle PSR\).
solution: \(m\angle PQR = \frac{1}{2} m(\text{arc PXR})\) ...(I) (inscribed angle theorem). \(m\angle PSR = \frac{1}{2} m(\text{arc PXR})\) ...(II) (inscribed angle theorem). \(\therefore m\angle PQR = m\angle PSR\) (from I and II). \(\therefore \angle PQR \cong \angle PSR\) (angles equal in measure are congruent).
figureNote: Circle through points P, Q, R, S with segments QR and PS drawn; \(\angle PQR\) and \(\angle PSR\) inscribed in the same arc, intercepting arc PXR (X on the lower circle) (page 3).

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: How many solid cylinders of radius 6 cm and height 12 cm can be made by melting a solid sphere of radius 18 cm?
solution: Radius of the sphere \(r = 18\) cm; for the cylinder, radius \(R = 6\) cm and height \(H = 12\) cm. Number of cylinders that can be made \(= \frac{\text{Volume of the sphere}}{\text{Volume of a solid cylinder}} = \frac{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{\pi R^2 H} = \frac{\frac{4}{3} \times 18 \times 18 \times 18}{6 \times 6 \times 12} = 18\) cylinders.

stem: In right-angled \(\triangle ABC\), \(BD \perp AC\). If \(AD = 4\) and \(DC = 9\), then find BD.
solution: In a right-angled triangle, the perpendicular drawn from the right angle to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two segments it makes, so \(BD^2 = AD \times DC\). \(BD^2 = 4 \times 9 = 36\), so \(BD = 6\).
figureNote: Right-angled \(\triangle ABC\) with the right angle at B; BD \(\perp\) hypotenuse AC (right angle marked at D), with AD = 4 and DC = 9 marked along AC (page 4).

stem: Verify whether the following points are collinear or not: A(1, -3), B(2, -5), C(-4, 7).
If \(\sec\theta = \frac{25}{7}\), then find the value of \(\tan\theta\).
solution: Using the identity \(1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta\), \(\tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta - 1 = \left(\frac{25}{7}\right)^2 - 1 = \frac{625}{49} - 1 = \frac{576}{49}\). \(\therefore \tan\theta = \frac{24}{7}\).

stem: In \(\triangle PQR\), seg PM is a median, \(PM = 9\) and \(PQ^2 + PR^2 = 290\). Find the length of QR.
solution: By Apollonius theorem, \(PQ^2 + PR^2 = 2PM^2 + 2QM^2\). \(290 = 2(9)^2 + 2QM^2 = 162 + 2QM^2\), so \(2QM^2 = 128\), \(QM^2 = 64\), \(QM = 8\). Since M is the midpoint of QR, \(QR = 2 \times QM = 2 \times 8 = 16\) units.

stem: In the given figure, O is the centre of the circle. \(\angle QPR = 70^\circ\) and \(m(\text{arc PYR}) = 160^\circ\), then find the value of each of the following: (a) m(arc QXR), (b) \(\angle QOR\), (c) \(\angle PQR\).
solution: (a) \(m(\text{arc QXR}) = 2\angle QPR = 2(70^\circ) = 140^\circ\) (inscribed angle theorem). (b) \(\angle QOR = m(\text{arc QXR}) = 140^\circ\) (the measure of an arc equals the measure of its central angle). (c) \(\angle PQR = \frac{1}{2} m(\text{arc PYR}) = \frac{1}{2}(160^\circ) = 80^\circ\) (inscribed angle theorem).
figureNote: Circle with centre O; points P, Q, R on the circle with Y between P and R (upper) and X below Q; \(\angle QPR = 70^\circ\) marked at P; seg OQ and seg OR drawn (page 5).

subtopic: Construction of a Tangent to a Circle
stem: Draw a circle with radius 4.2 cm. Construct tangents to the circle from a point at a distance of 7 cm from the centre.
solution: a. With radius 4.2 cm, draw a circle with centre O. b. Mark a point P such that \(d(O, P) = 7\) cm. c. Join OP and find its midpoint T using a perpendicular bisector. d. With T as centre and OT as radius, draw arcs cutting the circle at A and B (above and below OP). e. Join AP and BP; these are the required tangents.

stem: When an observer at a distance of 12 m from a tree looks at the top of the tree, the angle of elevation is \(60^\circ\). What is the height of the tree? \((\sqrt{3} = 1.73)\)
solution: Let CB be the height of the tree and the observer stand at A with \(\angle CAB = 60^\circ\) and \(BA = 12\) m. In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\tan 60^\circ = \frac{CB}{AB}\), so \(\sqrt{3} = \frac{CB}{12}\), giving \(CB = 12\sqrt{3} = 12 \times 1.73 = 20.76\) m.

subtopic: Tangent and Secant to a Circle
stem: A circle with centre P is inscribed in \(\triangle ABC\). Side AB, side BC and side AC touch the circle at points L, M and N respectively. The radius of the circle is r. Prove that \(A(\triangle ABC) = \frac{1}{2}(AB + BC + AC) \times r\).
solution: Construction: join PA, PL, PN, PC, PM and PB. Sides AB, BC and AC are tangents to the incircle (each touches it at a single point), and PL, PM, PN are radii. Since a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, \(PL \perp AB\), \(PM \perp BC\), \(PN \perp AC\), each equal to r. Then: \(A(\triangle APB) = \frac{1}{2} \times PL \times AB = \frac{1}{2} \times r \times AB\) ...(1); \(A(\triangle APC) = \frac{1}{2} \times r \times AC\) ...(2); \(A(\triangle BPC) = \frac{1}{2} \times r \times BC\) ...(3). Adding (1), (2) and (3), and using \(A(\triangle APB) + A(\triangle APC) + A(\triangle BPC) = A(\triangle ABC)\): \(A(\triangle ABC) = \frac{1}{2} \times r \times (AB + AC + BC) = \frac{1}{2}(AB + BC + AC) \times r\).
figureNote: \(\triangle ABC\) with an inscribed circle of centre P touching AB at L, BC at M and AC at N; radius r (page 4 statement, page 16 solution figure).

stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle ACB = 90^\circ\). Seg CD \(\perp\) side AB and seg CE is the angle bisector of \(\angle ACB\). Prove that \(\frac{AD}{BD} = \frac{AE^2}{BE^2}\).
solution: In \(\triangle ABC\), CD \(\perp\) AB. By similarity in a right-angled triangle, \(\triangle ACB \sim \triangle ADC\), so \(\frac{AC}{AD} = \frac{AB}{AC}\), which gives \(AC^2 = AB \times AD\). Also \(\triangle ACB \sim \triangle CDB\), so \(\frac{CB}{DB} = \frac{AB}{CB}\), which gives \(CB^2 = AB \times DB\). Since CE is the bisector of \(\angle ACB\), \(\frac{AC}{CB} = \frac{AE}{EB}\). Squaring both sides: \(\frac{AC^2}{CB^2} = \frac{AE^2}{EB^2}\). \(\therefore \frac{AB \times AD}{AB \times DB} = \frac{AE^2}{EB^2}\), i.e. \(\frac{AD}{BD} = \frac{AE^2}{BE^2}\).
figureNote: \(\triangle ABC\) with \(\angle ACB = 90^\circ\); seg CD \(\perp\) AB (right angle at D) and seg CE the bisector of \(\angle ACB\), with D and E on AB (page 5 statement, page 17 solution figure).

stem: Show that the points (2, 0), (-2, 0) and (0, 2) are the vertices of a triangle. Also state with reason the type of the triangle.
solution: Let A(2, 0), B(-2, 0), C(0, 2). By the distance formula: \(d(AB) = \sqrt{(2+2)^2 + (0-0)^2} = 4\); \(d(AC) = \sqrt{(2-0)^2 + (0-2)^2} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}\); \(d(BC) = \sqrt{(-2-0)^2 + (0-2)^2} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}\). The sum of any two of these distances is greater than the third, so A, B and C are the vertices of a triangle. Since \(d(AC) = d(BC)\) and \(AB^2 = 16 = 8 + 8 = AC^2 + BC^2\), \(\triangle ABC\) is an isosceles right-angled triangle.

subtopic: Area of Sector and Segment of a Circle
stem: In the figure, \(\square XLMT\) is a rectangle with \(LM = 21\) cm and \(XL = 10.5\) cm. The diameter of the smaller semicircle is half the diameter of the larger semicircle. Find the area of the non-shaded region.
solution: Let the diameter of the smaller semicircle be d; then the diameter of the larger semicircle is 2d. Since \(d + 2d = LM = 21\), we get \(3d = 21\), so \(d = 7\) cm. Area of smaller semicircle \(= \frac{\pi}{8}d^2 = \frac{22}{7} \times \frac{1}{8} \times 7^2 = 19.25\) cm\(^2\). Area of larger semicircle \(= \frac{\pi}{8}(2d)^2 = \frac{22}{7} \times \frac{1}{8} \times 14^2 = 77\) cm\(^2\). Area of rectangle \(= LM \times XL = 21 \times 10.5 = 220.5\) cm\(^2\). Area of shaded region \(=\) area of the two semicircles \(= 19.25 + 77 = 96.25\) cm\(^2\). Area of non-shaded region \(= 220.5 - 96.25 = 124.25\) cm\(^2\).
figureNote: Rectangle XLMT with LM = 21 cm and XL = 10.5 cm; a smaller shaded semicircle at the upper-left and a larger shaded semicircle at the lower-right, both drawn on the horizontal mid-line of the rectangle (page 6).
